units.la: Τὸ ποτήριον τῆς εὐλογίας ὃ εὐλογοῦμεν, οὐχὶ κοινωνία τοῦ αἵματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐστιν; τὸν ἄρτον ὃν κλῶμεν, οὐχὶ κοινωνία τοῦ σώματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐστιν;
units.tr: The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ [κοινωνία τοῦ αἵματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ]? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ [κοινωνία τοῦ σώματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ]?

units.la: Ὅτι εἷς ἄρτος, ἓν σῶμα οἱ πολλοί ἐσμεν. οἱ γὰρ πάντες ἐκ τοῦ ἑνὸς ἄρτου μετέχομεν.
units.tr: Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one bread [ἐκ τοῦ ἑνὸς ἄρτου μετέχομεν].

units.la: Ut prudentibus loquor. Judicate Vos quid dicam.
units.tr: I speak as to prudent men; judge you what I say.

units.la: Calix benedictionis cui benedicimus, nonne est communio sanguinis Christi? Panis quem frangimus, nonne est communio corporis Christi?
units.tr: The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?

units.la: Quia unus panis, unum corpus multi sumus. Omnes enim ex uno pane participamus.
units.tr: Because we, though many, are one bread and one body; for we all partake of the one bread.

units.la: THESIS I.
units.tr: THESIS I.

units.la: Textum hunc Apostolicum, in Argumentum Disputationis à Ven. Domino Praeside praescriptum, bono cum Deo enucleaturi, explicatis vocibus, modisque loquendi, qui occurrunt, analysin Logico-Theologicam trademus: post analysin enodabimus Quaestiones varias, ut sensus Textus melius patescat, quam parum faveat Adversariis, causam contra nostram contra illos egregie firmet: his peractis doctrinas inde fluentes breviter indigitabimus.
units.tr: Having this Apostolic text set down by the most reverend Praeses as the subject of the disputation, we will, with God's blessing, explain it. First we will set out a logical and theological analysis, unfolding the words and modes of speech that occur. After the analysis we will work through several questions so that the sense of the text may be more clearly seen, and so that it may firmly support our cause against the opponents, who it does little to favour. Having done this, we will briefly point out the doctrines that follow from it.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Quantum ad voces & phrases verfic.16. Poculum ponitur pro Vino in poculo, per Metonymiam subjecti pro adjuncto, cùm continens pro re contentâ sumitur: sic apud Horat.lib.1. ep.5.
units.tr: As to the words and phrases: verse 16 Cup is put for the wine in the cup, by metonymy of the subject for the adjunct, when the container is taken for what it contains. So in Horace, Epistles 1.5: Who has not been made eloquent by the fruitful cups?

units.la: Fœcundi calices quem non fecere disertum ? Calices i.e. Vinum in calicibus: & Virgil.lib.1. Æneid. de Bitia,
units.tr: Here cups, that is, the wine in the cups. And Virgil, Aeneid 1, of Bitias:

units.la: — — — — — — Ille Impiger hausit
units.tr: — — — — — — He eagerly drank

units.la: Spumantem paterám, & pleno se proluit auro.
units.tr: The foaming bowl, and washed himself in the full gold.

units.la: ὁ εὐλογῶμεν, proprie quod benedicimus: Beza reddit Cui benedicimus, quasi sit ὁ positum pro ᾧ. Chrysostomo εὐλογῶμεν idem est quod ἐπὶ ᾧ εὐχαριστοῦμεν, super quo gratias agimus.
units.tr: ὁ εὐλογῶμεν [ho eulogōmen], properly "which we bless." Beza renders it "to which we give blessing," as if ὁ were put for ᾧ. In Chrysostom, εὐλογῶμεν [eulogōmen] means the same as ἐπὶ ᾧ εὐχαριστοῦμεν [epi hō eucharistoumen], "over which we give thanks."

units.la: Κοινωνία, vox quæ alibi improprie beneficentiam denotat, hic est, pro nativa sua significatione, Communio.
units.tr: Κοινωνία [koinōnia], a word which elsewhere is used improperly for beneficence, here, in its native sense, means communion.

units.la: Τὸν ἄρτον ὃν κλῶμεν οὐχὶ κοινωνία &c. Panis quem frangimus nonne est &c. Latini ab hoc dicendi genere fere abhorrent. Illud enim Virgilii: Urbem quam statuo vestra est; plane Poeticum est. Occurrit & apud alios, sed rarius. Græci hac in parte imitantur Hebræos, quibus hæc Antiptosis usitatissima est. Similis habetur locutio Matth.21.42. ... Sic Marc.6.16. ... Rom.6.17. ... Viceversa Nominativus multoties ponitur vice reliquorum casuum: ut Joh.1.14. & 21.12. Eph.3.17,18. 2.Cor.9.11. 2.Pet.2.10. Apoc.1.5. Ita Luc.22.20. in hac ipsa materia: Τοῦτο τὸ ποτήριον, ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη ἐν τῷ αἵματί μου, τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἐκχυνόμενον, pro τῷ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἐκχυνομένῳ. Et sic facilis est responsio ad argumentum Transsubstantiatorum & Consubstantiatorum ex hoc loco: Calicem non denotare tantùm Calicem, sed & sanguinem in Calice; cùm de calice dicatur, quod pro nobis effusus sit. Non enim hoc de Calice dicitur, substantivo remotiore; sed de sanguine substantivo propiore, per Antiptosin.
units.tr: Τὸν ἄρτον ὃν κλῶμεν οὐχὶ κοινωνία [ton artov hon klōmen ouchi koinōnia] etc., "The bread which we break, is it not a communion" etc. Latin writers mostly shrink from this kind of expression. That line of Virgil, The city which I am founding is yours, is quite poetic. It occurs also with other writers, but more rarely. The Greeks in this matter imitate the Hebrews, among whom this antiptosis is most common. A similar construction is found in Matthew 21.42 ... so in Mark 6.16 ... Romans 6.17 ... Conversely, the nominative is often put in place of the other cases, as in John 1.14, 21.12; Ephesians 3.17, 18; 2 Corinthians 9.11; 2 Peter 2.10; Revelation 1.5. So also Luke 22.20, in this very matter: Τοῦτο τὸ ποτήριον, ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη ἐν τῷ αἵματί μου, τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἐκχυνόμενον [touto to potērion, hē kainē diathēkē en tō haimati mou, to hyper hymōn ekchynomenon], where the sense requires τῷ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἐκχυνομένῳ [tō hyper hymōn ekchynomenō]. And so there is an easy answer to the argument of the Transubstantiationists and Consubstantiationists from this passage, that the cup means not only the cup but also the blood in the cup, since it is said of the cup that it was poured out for us. For this is not said of the cup, a more distant noun, but of the blood, the nearer noun, by antiptosis.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Progredimur ad Analysin. Apostolus adhuc in eo est, ut dehortetur ab usu Idolothytorum publico, accubituque cum Idololatris in epulis sacris. Esum istum & Communionem cum Idololatris, versu præcedente, Idololatriam esse dixit, adeoque que fugiendam: Idololatriam enimDeo contumeliosam esse, ac eapropter graviter puniri, quod exemplo Israelitarum in deserto pereuntium illustravit. Nunc aliud argumentum inde depromit,quod qui epulentur cum Idololatris in Templis, in Communionem Dæmoniorum ipsorum transeant: Probat hoc à pari vel contrario: ut enim Eucharistia sit Communio Christi, ita epulas tales earumque participationem esse Communionem Diabolorum.
units.tr: We proceed to the analysis. The Apostle is still engaged in dissuading from the public eating of things sacrificed to idols and from reclining with idolaters at sacred feasts. In the preceding verse he called this eating and communion with idolaters idolatry, and therefore to be shunned, since idolatry is an insult to God and for that reason is severely punished, as he illustrated by the example of the Israelites who perished in the desert. Now he draws another argument from this, that those who feast with idolaters in their temples pass into communion with the demons themselves. He proves this from a like or from a contrary case: just as the Eucharist is the communion of Christ, so such feasts and the participation in them are the communion of devils.

units.la: Partes Textus duæ: 1. Præfatiuncula, 2. Ipsum Argumentum.
units.tr: The text has two parts: (1) the short preface; (2) the argument itself.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Præfatiuncula continetur verbis: Ut prudentibus loquor, judicate vos ipsi quid dicam.
units.tr: The preface is contained in the words: As I speak to prudent people, judge for yourselves what I say.

units.la: Accommodata est tùm ad captandam benevolentiam, tùm ad parandam attentionem. Defert ipsis Corinthiis judicium eorum, quæ dicturus sit.
units.tr: It is suited both to win goodwill and to secure attention. He hands to the Corinthians themselves the judgment of what he is about to say.

units.la: Delationis autem istius notanda. 1. Ratio. 2. Modus.
units.tr: In this handing over we should note two things: (1) the reason; (2) the manner.

units.la: Ratio à prudentia eorum desumpta, ac proin laudatoria est.
units.tr: The reason is drawn from their prudence, and is therefore a commendation.

units.la: Ut prudentibus loquor: quasi dicat: quia novi vos prudentes i.e. satis edoctos esse, de mysteriorum horum naturâ, non dubito vobis judicium committere, bonâ spe fretus, sententiam secuturam talem, quæ prudentiam & pietatem vestram deceat, mihique adstipulatura sit.
units.tr: As I speak to prudent people: as if he said, "Because I know you to be prudent, that is, sufficiently taught about the nature of these mysteries, I do not hesitate to commit the judgment to you, relying on the good hope that the verdict will be such as befits your prudence and piety, and will agree with me."

units.la: Modus delationis postulatorius aut imperativus est: Judicate vos ipsi: Ubi notentur Personæ ad quas provocat. Vos ipsi: Ut & opus, quod exigit, judicium videl. Judicate: quod ab Objecto describitur, quod dico.
units.tr: The manner of handing over is a request or command: Judge for yourselves. Here we note the persons to whom he appeals: yourselves; and also the work which he demands, namely judgment: judge; which is described by its object: what I say.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Sequitur Argur. entum ipsum: Nonne Calix est Communio &c. Notandus hic Modus loquendi & Res ipsa.
units.tr: Next comes the argument itself: Is not the cup a communion, etc. Here we note the mode of speech and the thing itself.

units.la: Modus loquendi Interrogatorius: Nonne est Calix?
units.tr: The mode of speech is interrogative: Is not the cup?

units.la: Res ipsa huc redit: in Cœnâ esse Communionem fidelium 1. cum Christo. 2. inter ipsos invicem.
units.tr: The thing itself comes to this: that in the Supper there is a communion of believers (1) with Christ; (2) with one another.

units.la: Quod attinet ad Communionem fidelium cum Christo, de ea loquitur secundùm duas Cœnæ partes: quippe quâ ciba-mur, & potamur. v.16. Circa priorem partem notanda tùm signum tùm res signata. De signo ait : Calix benedictionis cui benedicimus : Indigitat substantiam, quæ Calix sive Vinum & Actionem sacramentalem circa Calicem, quæ benedictio est. Res signata exprimitur verbis: Communio sanguinis Christi est. Ubi Modus notatur nomine Communionis : Objectum nomine sanguinis Christi.
units.tr: As regards the communion of believers with Christ, he speaks of it according to the two parts of the Supper, by which we are fed and drink (v. 16). With regard to the first part we should note both the sign and the thing signified. Of the sign he says: The cup of blessing which we bless. It points to the substance, which is the cup or wine, and to the sacramental action performed over the cup, which is the blessing. The thing signified is expressed in the words: It is the communion of the blood of Christ. Here the mode is noted by the word communion, and the object by the words blood of Christ.

units.la: Quod ad alteram Cœnæ partem attinet, consideranda veniunt pariter Signum, & Res signata. De signo ita loquitur: Panis quem frangimus : Notatur substantia, quæ panis ; & Actio sive Ritus sacramentalis, qui Fractio est. Res signata habetur verbis Communio corporis Christi est. Ubi Modus nomine Koinonias & Objectum nomine corporis significatur.
units.tr: As to the other part of the Supper, the sign and the thing signified likewise come under consideration. Of the sign he speaks thus: The bread which we break. Here is noted the substance, which is bread, and the action or sacramental rite, which is the breaking. The thing signified is contained in the words It is the communion of the body of Christ. Here the mode is signified by the noun koinonia [κοινωνία], and the object by the word body.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: De Communione fidelium inter se agit v.17. Quoniam unus panis &c. Notanda hic 1. Connexio cum præcedentibus per particulam causalem quoniam. 2. Propositio : Unus Panis &c. Ubi signum, Unus Panis : Res signata, Unum Corpus nos multi. 3. Ratio his verbis indigitata : Nam omnes ex uno illo pane participamus.
units.tr: Here he treats of the communion of the faithful among themselves, at 1 Cor. 10:17, "Since there is one bread," etc. Three things are to be noted here: 1. the connection with what precedes, through the causal particle "since" (quoniam); 2. the proposition: "one bread," etc., where the sign is "one bread" and the thing signified is "we, many, are one body"; 3. the reason indicated by these words: "For we all partake of that one bread."

units.la: Excussâ horum verborum analysi, transeamus ad Quæstiones primùm Textuales, subinde Controversas.
units.tr: Having gone through the analysis of these words, let us pass on to the questions, first the textual ones, and afterwards the controverted ones.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Quæstio Textualis I. Qui vocet Apostolus hic prudentes, quos supra cap.3,2. nominavit Carnales & Infantes?
units.tr: Textual Question I. Whom does the Apostle here call the prudent, whom he named carnal and infants above in 3:2?

units.la: 1. Erant Carnales affectibus, quatenus contenderunt de Ministris suis, & secundùm diversam illorum qualitatem sciderunt Ecclesiam in sectas. In præsenti verò causâ, à priori longè diversa, appellat eos prudentes, ob scientiâ doctrinæ, quatenùs cæteris in causâ fidei instructiores fuerat, licèt non meliores. Quare nihil est hic contradictionis : constat enim scientissimos sæpe Doctores carnalibus affectibus indulgere maximè. 2. Non omnes Corinthii erant carnales, nec omnes prudentes, sed alii & alii tales. Alios igitur hic, & alios ibi intelligit. Sæpè enim, quod alialiquorum saltem est in coetu, toti coetui indefinitè tribuitur.
units.tr: 1. They were carnal in their affections, in that they quarrelled about their ministers, and according to the different quality of those ministers they split the Church into sects. In the present case, however, which is quite different from the earlier one, he calls them prudent because of their knowledge of doctrine, in that they were better instructed than the others in the cause of faith, though not better men. Hence there is no contradiction here, for it is well established that very learned teachers often indulge their carnal affections most of all. 2. Not all the Corinthians were carnal, nor all prudent, but some were one and some another. He therefore means some here and others there. For what belongs to some part at least of the assembly is often attributed indefinitely to the whole assembly.

units.la: VIII. Quæstio II. Quomodo judicium Apostolus nunc iis deferat, quos supra judicare vetuerat 1.Cor.4,5.
units.tr: VIII. Question II. How does the Apostle now refer to judgment those whom he had forbidden above to judge? 1 Cor. 4:5.

units.la: Ne ante tempus quicquam judicate?
units.tr: Judge nothing before the time?

units.la: Paulus superius prohibuit judicia intempestiva. Annexuit enim προ καιρῶν, Ante tempus; & affectata de rebus ignotis. Hic vero requirit judicium verum de rebus merito notissimis. Non igitur haec pugnant.
units.tr: The Apostle earlier forbade untimely judgments. For he added before the time [προ καιρῶν], and presumptuous judgments about unknown matters. Here, however, he requires true judgment about matters that are rightly very well known. Therefore these do not conflict.

units.la: IX. Quæstio III. Cur interrogative loquatur Apostolus, Nonne?
units.tr: IX. Question III. Why does the Apostle speak interrogatively, "Is it not?"

units.la: Vulgò respondetur: Interrogativas hujusmodi locutiones negativas fortiter affirmare. Nonne est Communio? h.e. Utique, sine dubio est Communio. Contrà affirmativas negare. Ut: Num injustus est Deus? i.e. nulla ratione injustus est. Rom.3,5. Addimus & hoc, cum Apostolo visum sit judicium deferre Corinthiis, eum ita loqui & interrogatione uti, par fuisse, Nonne est? q.d. nihil definiam ipse, sed judicium & responsum vestrum expectabo.
units.tr: It is commonly answered that such interrogative expressions strongly affirm a negative: Is there not communion? that is, of course, there is communion, without doubt. Conversely, they deny an affirmative, as: Is God unjust? that is, he is in no way unjust, Rom. 3:5. We add also that, since the Apostle thought fit to leave the judgment to the Corinthians, it was fitting that he speak in this way and use a question, "Is it not?" as if to say: I myself will define nothing, but I will await your judgment and answer.

units.la: X. Quæstio IV. Cur Apostolus initium faciat à Calice, cum secundum ordinem Institutionis Dominicæ Panis precedere deberet?
units.tr: X. Question IV. Why does the Apostle begin with the cup, when according to the order of the Lord's institution the bread ought to come first?

units.la: Hic variæ variorum sunt sententiæ. Sunt qui dicant inde factum, quod Calix potior sit Coenæ pars. Nam vinum sanguinem denotare, panem corpus sive carnem. Animam autem in sanguine esse existimant, qui proin corpore & carne nobilior sit. Verùm qui sic sentiunt, non vident se Christum incogitantiæ arguere, quòd non & ipse habitâ hujus dignitatis ratione, de Poculo prius, dein de Pane constituerit. Sunt, qui existiment, hoc datum Hebræorum consuetudisuetudini, qui soleant in Conviviis solennibus à poculo gratiarum actionem auspicari: Et huc facere putant quod Luc.22.17. prius poculi mentio fiat, quàm panis. At nec mos Hebræorum exemplo nobis in Cænâ Domini esse debet: nec poculum illud Judaici Paschatis, cujus prior fit mentio, ad Mysterium pertinebat, quod erat post illud separatim instituendum à Domino; sed ad ritum Vet. Paschatis. Causa equidem hæc anxiè disquirenda non est. Si qua tamen danda, hæc erit, quod mens Apostoli fuit, paulo fusius de Pane, quàm de Poculo loqui: proin ultimò de eo dicere constituit. Sic Apoc.1.4.5. Johannes non observato Ordine Trinitatis, Filio, Sp.S. præponit, quia de Filio, ut Mediatore & Prophetiæ hujus revelatore, plura dicturus erat.
units.tr: Here opinions of various men differ. Some say that this was done because the cup is the more excellent part of the Supper, since wine denotes the blood and bread the body or flesh. They think the soul is in the blood, and so is nobler than body and flesh. But those who think this way do not see that they accuse Christ of thoughtlessness, since he did not himself, having regard to this dignity, institute first the cup and then the bread. Some think that this was given to the custom of the Hebrews, who are wont to begin thanksgiving at solemn feasts with the cup, and they think that this favours the fact that in Luke 22:17 mention of the cup comes before that of the bread. But the custom of the Hebrews ought not to be a model for us in the Lord's Supper, nor did that cup of the Jewish Passover, of which mention comes first, belong to the Mystery, which was to be instituted separately by the Lord afterwards, but to the rite of the Old Passover. Indeed, this matter need not be anxiously investigated. If some reason is to be given, it will be this: the mind of the Apostle was to speak somewhat more fully of the bread than of the cup, and so he determined to speak of it last. Thus in Rev. 1:4-5 John, not observing the order of the Trinity, puts the Son before the Holy Spirit, because he was about to say more about the Son, as Mediator and as the revealer of this prophecy.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Quæstio V. Quomodo reddenda sit εὐλογία, an per Benedictionem vel Gratiarum Actionem an Consecrationem?
units.tr: Question V. How is eulogia [εὐλογία] to be rendered: as blessing, or thanksgiving, or consecration?

units.la: §. Calvinus vertendam esse per Consecrationem judicat. Verba ejus hæc sunt: Neque enim his assentior qui per Benedictionem gratiarum actionem intelligunt, & benedicere exponunt gratias agere: & paulo post, Benedicere ergo Calicem significat in hunc Usum consecrare, ut nobis sit symbolum sanguinis Domini. Hæc ille. Coincidit Bezæ interpretatio, qui existimat, verbum εὐλογεῖν idem hic declarare ac infinitis locis V.T. verbum קדש i.e. ἁγιάζειν ἢ καθιερῶν, sanctificare seu consecrare, quia symbola hæc, Panis & Vinum, à communi usu sequestrata ad sacrum destinantur.
units.tr: Calvin judges that it should be rendered as consecration. His words are these: For I do not agree with those who understand it as blessing in the sense of giving thanks, and who explain "to bless" as "to give thanks." And a little later: To bless the cup, therefore, means to consecrate it to this use, so that it may be for us a symbol of the blood of the Lord. So he. Beza's interpretation agrees with this. He thinks that the verb eulogein [εὐλογεῖν] here means the same as the Hebrew verb qadash [קדש] in countless places of the Old Testament, that is, hagiazein [ἁγιάζειν] or katieroun [καθιερῶν], to sanctify or to consecrate, because these symbols, bread and wine, are withdrawn from common use and destined for the sacred.

units.la: Bullingerus vult, non aliter reddi posse, quàm per gratiarum Actionem. Sic Agenda Palatina, der Kelch der Danckfagung/ damit wir danckfagen.
units.tr: Bullinger holds that it can be rendered in no other way than by thanksgiving. So too the Palatine Agenda: "the cup of thanksgiving" (der Kelch der Danckfagung), "so that we give thanks."

units.la: Hæc conciliaturus Petrus Martyr statuit, ex duplici hac expositione, haud difficulter Unam conflari: dum enim inquit, gratias Deo agimus, & commemora- mus mus quæ bona per Christum dederit & promiserit, habetur ea, quam isti appellant consecrationem: adeoq; Paulum verbo hoc εὐλογίαν totam hanc Actionem expressisse putamus.
units.tr: Petrus Martyr, wishing to reconcile these two explanations, holds that one can easily be formed out of these two interpretations: for while we give thanks to God, and recall the good things which he has given and promised through Christ, there is present that which they call consecration. And so we think that Paul by this word εὐλογίαν expressed this whole action.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Quæstio VI. Quomodo v. 17. cohæreat cum præcedente?
units.tr: Question 6. How does verse 17 cohere with what precedes?

units.la: Connectitur per particulam ὅτι, Quoniam. Quoniam unus panis &c. Non adeò planum videtur, quomodo Apostolus, Panem esse Communionem Corporis Christi, inde probet: quòd nos invicem Unum Corpus Mysticum sumus. Cohærentia nobis videtur esse talis: Apostolus dehortatur ab esu Idolothytorum, & accubitu cum Ethnicis in epulis sacris, quòd per illum habeant communionem cum Idolis, quibus cibi isti fuerint immolati; & cum Idololatris, quibus cum edant ac bibant. Probat utrumque à pari sive potius opposito: Prius, quòd in Cœnâ Panis sit communio Corporis Christi, h.e. qui edunt panem, quem opponit Idolothytis, participent Corpus Christi, quod opponit Idolis ipsis. Posterius probat inde, quia Unum Corpus mysticum sint, qui unà communicent. E. etiam qui in Idolis unà edunt, Communionem invicem habere.
units.tr: It is connected by the particle ὅτι, "since" (quoniam). "Since there is one bread," etc. It does not seem altogether plain how the Apostle proves from this that bread is the communion of the body of Christ: namely, because we are one mystical body together. The connection, as it seems to me, is this. The Apostle dissuades from eating things sacrificed to idols and from reclining with the Gentiles at sacred feasts, because through these they have communion with the idols to which the foods were offered, and with the idolaters with whom they eat and drink. He proves both by a parallel, or rather by an opposite. The first point: in the Supper there is communion in the body of Christ, that is, those who eat the bread, which he sets against things sacrificed to idols, partake of the body of Christ, which he sets against the idols themselves. The second point he proves from this, because those who partake together are one mystical body; therefore those who eat together in the idols also have communion with one another.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Quæstio VII. Quis genuinus sit versus hujus sensus?
units.tr: Question VII. What is the genuine meaning of this verse?

units.la: Communio fidelium inter se hoc versu partim explicatur, partim probatur. Explicatur, quòd, perinde ut Panis Eucharisticus, etsi cum frangitur, in multas particulas dividatur; unus est Panis: Ita etiam omnes communicantes, ut maximè eorum sint multi, unum sint corpus Mysticum. Unus Panis, unum corpus multi sumus. Probatur hæc Communio inde, quia omnes ex Uno pane participant. Cùm videmus plures ad eandem mensam eodem pane vesci, colligimus hinc, esse aliquam inter hos unà edentes Communionem & Societatem. Hinc est, quòd Companis vel Companionis vocabulum pro socio ponitur, & Græcorum σύωπιτ​@ proprie significans, qui cibum unà sumit seu Convictorem, pro sodali quoque accipiatur. Ita & hoc, quòd in Cœna omnes de eodem pane participant, argumentum est Communionis & Unitatis eorum. Huc refer quæ Eph.4.3,4,5. habentur.
units.tr: In this verse the communion of the faithful with one another is partly explained and partly proved. It is explained thus: just as the Eucharistic bread, although it is broken and divided into many pieces, remains one bread, so all who communicate, however many they are, are one mystical body. One bread, one body, we who are many. The communion is proved from the fact that all partake of the one bread. When we see several people eating from the same bread at the same table, we infer that there is some communion and fellowship among those who eat together. Hence the word companion, or messmate, is used for a comrade, and the Greek [σύσσιτος], which properly means one who eats his food with another, is also taken to mean a friend. So too, the fact that in the Supper all partake of the same bread is an argument for their communion and unity. Refer here what is said in Eph.4.3, 4, 5.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Hactenus Quæstiones Textuales: Succedunt Controversæ: quarum prima numero, ordine VIII. hæc est: An ex v.15. rectè probetur. Usus Rationis in rebus Theologicis & fidei?
units.tr: So far the textual questions. Now follow the controversies, of which the first, in number and order the eighth, is this: Whether from v. 15 it is rightly proved that reason has a use in theological matters and in faith?

units.la: Ꝟ. Lutherani non habentes, quod reponant nostris rationibus contra Ubiquitatem & Consubstantiationem, clamitant: Rationem in rebus fidei non audiendam, neque ferre possunt Axioma vulgare: Mysteria Religionis esse supra Rationem, non contra illam. Ita qui inter Pontificios Methodum Veronianam contra Hæreticos disputandi amplectuntur, consequentias omninò rejiciunt hoc nomine, quod fidei dogmata non rationis discursu, sed revelationis certitudine nitantur. Facile agnoscimus, Rationem non esse principium Religionis, esse tamen ejus aliquem hic usum, patet ex hac Apostoli postulatione: Judicate &c. ministerialem videl. non Principalem. Captivanda utique Ratio sub obsequium fidei; 2. Cor. 10.5. sed omnem Rationis usum rejicere, est eam non captivare sed exuere; Hagaram, etiam modestam & ancillantem, ejicere; &, cùm ad cotem novacula exacui deberet, novaculâ Cotem dissecare.
units.tr: The Lutherans, having nothing to set against our arguments against ubiquity and consubstantiation, cry out that reason is not to be heard in matters of faith. They cannot accept the common axiom: the mysteries of religion are above reason, not against it. Likewise those among the Papists who embrace the Veronian method of disputing against heretics reject consequences altogether on this ground, that the dogmas of faith rest not on the reasoning of reason but on the certainty of revelation. We readily acknowledge that reason is not the principle of religion, yet that it has some use here is clear from this demand of the Apostle: Judge &c. — a ministerial use, namely, not a principal one. Reason indeed must be taken captive to the obedience of faith (2 Cor. 10.5); but to reject all use of reason is not to take it captive but to strip it naked; it is to cast out Hagar, even when she is modest and serving; and, when reason ought to be sharpened on the whetstone like a razor, it is to cut the whetstone with the razor.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Quæstio IX. An ex eodem v. contra Pontificios rectè probemus judicium discretionis, quòd Laici, ut loquuntur, doctrinam sibi propositam absque examine & judicio non debeant recipere?
units.tr: Question IX. Whether from the same verse we may rightly prove against the Papists the judgment of discernment, that the laity, as they say, ought not to accept doctrine proposed to them without examination and judgment?

units.la: Ꝟ. Argumentum pro judicio discretionis suppeditat nobis Apostolus, judicate vos Ipsi quid dicam. Requirit, ut judicent de iis quæ dicturus esset, adeoque judicium discrediscretivum de doctrinâ suâ Corinthiis concedit, imò imperat. Sunt adhuc plura alia loca, quibus expressum hoc mandatum legitur, ut 1.Cor.11.13. Apud Vos Ipsos judicate. Matt.24.4. Videte ne quis vos seducat. 1.Theff.5.21. Omnia probate. 1.Joh.4.1. Nolite cuivis Spiritui credere, sed probate Spiritus an ex Deo sint. Et hoc nomine laudantur Beroënses Act.17.11. Hinc certè sequitur, omninò adhibendum judicium discretivum. Absq; hoc enim, quomodo observabitur Pauli monitum, κείνατε ὁ φησί? quomodo cavebitur seductio, si contingat, eum, qui Ecclesiae praeest, falsâ imbutum esse doctrinâ; auditor verò doctrinis & definitionibus ejus, sine omni examine, tantùm propter authoritatem officii ejus, fidem adhibere teneatur? quomodo probabuntur Spiritus, si judicare de spirituum doctrinis nefas fuerit?
units.tr: The Apostle supplies us with an argument for the judgment of discernment: judge ye yourselves what I say [κρίνατε ὃ φημί]. He requires them to judge what he was about to say, and so he grants the Corinthians a discerning judgment about his teaching; indeed, he commands it. Several other passages also read this command expressly: 1 Cor. 11.13. Judge among yourselves. Matt. 24.4. Take heed that no one deceive you. 1 Thess. 5.21. Prove all things. 1 John 4.1. Believe not every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are of God. The Bereans are also praised for this very thing, Acts 17.11. From this it certainly follows that a discerning judgment must be employed without exception. For without it, how will Paul's warning be observed, "I speak as to wise men; judge what I say"? How will seduction be guarded against, if it happens that he who presides over the Church has been imbued with false doctrine, while the hearer is bound to give faith to his teachings and definitions without any examination, merely because of the authority of his office? How will the spirits be proved, if it were wrong to judge the doctrines of spirits?

units.la: Respondet Bellarminus; agi locis citatis de doctrinâ dubiâ; qua indigeat probatione: doctrinam autem legitimorum Praepositorum non esse dubiam, sed aperte bonam. Atqui constat, Ministros Vocationem ordinariam & legitimam habentes, doctrinas interdum aperte falsas proposuisse. Quid enim? An Sacerdotes, de quorum corruptelis Prophetae conqueruntur; An Doctores, quorum ψευδεπιμνείας ipse Servator subvertit; An Arius, Nestorius, Eutyches non fuerunt Doctores, legitimè vocati? constat tamen, perniciosissimos errores ab ipsis propositos fuisse. Et, si licuit judicare de doctrinâ ipsorum Apostolorum, Ministrorum extraordinariorum & infallibilium, quanto magis de ordinariorum & fallibilium doctrinâ judicare licitum, imò necessarium erit? Doctrina illorum, etsi in se certissima, auditori tamen indubia non est, donec Scripturae Propheticae & Apostolicae examussim congruere cognoscitur.
units.tr: Bellarmine replies that the passages cited concern doubtful doctrine, which needs proof; but the doctrine of lawful prelates is not doubtful, but plainly good. Yet it is evident that ministers who had an ordinary and lawful call have sometimes proposed plainly false doctrines. For what of it? Were the priests, about whose corruptions the prophets complain, not such? Were the teachers whose false [ψευδεπιμνείας] the Saviour himself overthrew not such? Were Arius, Nestorius and Eutyches not teachers, lawfully called? Yet it is certain that they put forward most pernicious errors. And if it was lawful to judge the doctrine of the apostles themselves, who were extraordinary and infallible ministers, how much more lawful, indeed how much more necessary, will it be to judge the doctrine of ordinary and fallible ministers? Their doctrine, though in itself most certain, is nevertheless not indubitable to the hearer, until it is known to agree exactly with the prophetic and apostolic Scriptures.

units.la: Secundò respondet Bellarmin. Praedicta mandata non ad omnes, sed ad Doctores solos pertinere: sicut inquit, si scribitur ad aliquam Academiam, ut examinet librum, non ille examinandus est promiscuè ab omnibus, sed tantùm à Doctoribus ejus Facultatis, de quâ liber tractat, tractat. Ita Deus mandat, ut Præpositi, non ut Laici judicent, Spiritus probent, & doctrinas examinent. At verò, si ita res habet, sequetur, inter Corinthios solos Doctores aut Clericos, ut illi loquuntur, idolothyta comedisse, & cum infidelibus ἐν τῷ εἰδωλείῳ accubuisse; Eos enim, qui hoc fecerant, adhuc alloquitur. Sequetur, solius Cleri esse, observare τὰς κοπιῶντας ἐν πρωϊγαμένας ἐν Κυρίῳ, eosque quàm maximè charos ducere; cùm tamen auditoribus hoc dari præceptum, per se pateat. Sequetur, solum Clerum aut Ecclesiæ Doctores vocari Johanni τεκνία, puerulos, cùm tamen hæc appellatio multo aptius competat privatis fidelibus, quàm Doctoribus aut Præpositis.
units.tr: Secondly, Bellarmine replies: the aforesaid commands pertain not to all, but to teachers alone; just as, he says, if it is written to some academy that it should examine a book, that book is not to be examined indiscriminately by everyone, but only by the teachers of the faculty with which the book deals. So God commands that prelates, not laymen, judge, prove the spirits and examine the doctrines. But if this is so, it will follow that among the Corinthians only the teachers, or the clergy as they call them, ate food sacrificed to idols and reclined with unbelievers in an idol's temple [ἐν τῷ εἰδωλείῳ]; for he still addresses those who had done this. It will follow that only the clergy are to observe those who labour among you and are over you in the Lord [τοὺς κοπιῶντας ἐν ὑμῖν καὶ προϊσταμένους ὑμῶν ἐν Κυρίῳ] and to hold them in the highest esteem, although it is plain in itself that this precept is given to the hearers. It will follow that only the clergy or teachers of the Church are called by John little children [τεκνία], little ones, although this name fits private faithful far more aptly than teachers or prelates.

units.la: Possemus quoque Testimonia Veterum, Hieronymi, Augustini aliorumque Eximiorum Theologorum pro judicio hoc discretivo ab omnibus adhibendo huc apponere, nisi breviores esse constituissemus. Plura qui desiderat, consulat Virum Reverendiss. Joh. Davenantium, in eximio Opere de Judice Controversiarum.
units.tr: We could also set down here the testimonies of the Ancients, of Jerome, Augustine and other eminent theologians, in support of this discerning judgment to be employed by all, had we not decided to be briefer. Whoever desires more should consult the most reverend John Davenant, in his excellent work on the Judge of Controversies.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Quæstio X. An recte ex hoc loco probetur, Romanam Ecclesiam injustè Laicis, quos vocant, calicem ademisse?
units.tr: Question X. Whether it is rightly proved from this passage that the Roman Church unjustly took the cup away from the so-called laity?

units.la: In Ecclesiâ Corinthiacâ Eucharistiam sub utraque specie sive symbolo dispensatam, calicéq; non minùs quàm Panem omnibus oblatum fuisse, patet ex hoc loco, ut & ex iis quæ infra v.21. habentur, Non potestis simul, &c. Praxin istam Christi instituto & exemplo ad amussim fuisse conformem, probant ea quæ c.11. v.25. sequuntur. Dici non potest, Apostolum saltem respicere Sacerdotes, cùm de Calice loquitur. Nam fideles in genere intelligit, cùm dicit, Non potestis Calicem Domini bibere, & Calicem Damoniorum. Item cùm dicit, quosdam à Deo punitos, quòd indignè tàm de Calice bibissent, quàm de pane manducassent.
units.tr: That in the Corinthian Church the Eucharist was dispensed under both kinds or symbols, and the cup was offered to all no less than the bread, is clear from this passage, and also from what is found below at v. 21: You cannot drink, &c. That this practice was entirely in accordance with the institution and example of Christ is shown by what follows in chapter 11, v. 25. It cannot be said that the Apostle is referring only to the priests when he speaks of the cup. For he means the faithful in general when he says, You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. Likewise, when he says that certain people were punished by God because they had received unworthily both the cup and the bread.

units.la: Excipiunt aliqui: In Ecclesia Corinthiacâ hunc morem obtinuisse, sed in Ecclesiâ Hierosolymitanâ aliter factum: Opponunt, Jacobum sub Unâ administrantem, Paulo administranti sub utraque. Jacobum sub una administrasse probant ex Act.2.42.46.
units.tr: Some object: that this custom prevailed in the Corinthian Church, but that things were done differently in the Church of Jerusalem. They set against Paul, who administered under both kinds, James, who administered under one kind. They prove that James administered under one kind from Acts 2.42, 46.

units.la: Ꝛ. Si maximè concedamus, quod non omnibus est verisimile, hic Cœnam intelligi, in promptu est responsio. Sicut aliàs sub Panis nomine continetur omne, quod ad refectionem est necessarium Gen.43.25. Ita & cùm de Cœna sermo, nomine Panis etiam Vinum per Synecdochen indigitatur, adeoque tota Cœna. Aut admittunt Pontificii hanc Synecdochen, aut non admittunt. Si admittunt, periit vis argumenti. Si non admittunt, sequetur non saltem Laicos, sed & Conficientes sub unâ specie communicasse.
units.tr: Answer: Even if we grant, which is not altogether probable, that the Supper is meant here, the reply is ready to hand. Just as elsewhere everything that is necessary for sustenance is included under the name bread (Gen. 43.25), so also when the discussion is of the Supper, wine is indicated by the name bread by synecdoche, and so the whole Supper is meant. Either the Papists admit this synecdoche or they do not. If they admit it, the force of the argument is lost. If they do not admit it, it will follow that not only the laity but also the consecrating priests received under one kind only.

units.la: Objiciunt. Satis esse, Corporis symbolum tradi. Sic enim cum Carne & sanguinem, qui sit in carne, & detur cum symbolo carnis per concomitantiam communicari.
units.tr: Objection. It is enough that the symbol of the Body be given, for in this way the blood, which is in the flesh, is received together with the flesh, and is given with the symbol of the flesh by concomitance.

units.la: Ꝛ. Dum hoc dicunt, sibi sapientiores videntur ipso Christo, quasi superfluum fuisset, quòd sanguinis symbolum seorsim in Calice instituerit. Cœna est instituta in commemorationem sacrificii Christi propitiatorij, quod sine sanguinis fusione fieri non potuit Heb.9.22. seu, quod idem, in memoriam passionis, quâ Corpus ejus fractum & sanguis fusus. Panis itaque symbolum Corporis non vivi, sed fracti, h.e. exanimis & exanguis; & Vinum sanguinis, non in venis contenti, sed extra corpus profusi.
units.tr: Answer: In saying this, they seem to themselves wiser than Christ himself, as if it had been superfluous for him to institute separately in the cup the symbol of the blood. The Supper was instituted in remembrance of the propitiatory sacrifice of Christ, which could not be made without the shedding of blood (Heb. 9.22); or, what is the same, in memory of the passion, by which his body was broken and his blood poured out. Therefore the bread is the symbol of a body not living but broken, that is, lifeless and bloodless; and the wine is the symbol of blood not contained in the veins but poured out from the body.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Quæstio IX. An Pontificii ex h. l. recte probent Transsubstantiationem?
units.tr: Question IX. Do the Papists rightly prove Transubstantiation from this passage?

units.la: Pontificii εὐλογίαν benedictionem interpretantur Consecrationem, quæ juxta illos fit demurmuratione quinque horum verborum, Hoc enim est sanguis meus. Item: Hoc est enim Corpus meum. Horum vi volunt vinum in sanguinem & panem in corpus Christi transsubstantiari. Sic Lyra & Dionysius: Cui benedicimus, h. e. quem consecramus nos Sacerdotes, cum per prolationem sacrorum verborum à nobis in sanguinem Christi convertitur. Pro hac Consecratione citant Irenæum, Ambrosium, Cyrillum &c. Adhæc Resp. 1: Glossam hanc de Consecratione, quam vocant, conversivâ, salsissimam esse, ut & ineptissimam. Qui enim hæc cohærent? Calix i.e. sanguis in Calice; cui benedicimus,i.e.quem consecratione convertimus in sanguinem,est communio sanguinis: quid quaeso hac glossa ineptius? 2. Agnoscimus Veteres interdum sic loqui,panem per consecrationem mutari in corpus Christi: id vero non de mutatione aliqua essentiali, qua substantia Panis in substantiam Corporis convertatur,intelligendum est; sed de mutatione mystica & Sacramentali, qua, interventu benedictionis & consecrationis,Panis & Vinum ita mutantur,ut quae prius erant communia & profana,incipiant esse sacra, adeoque ex communibus vulgatisque mutentur & convertantur in sacra, quod consensus Antiquitatis Orthodoxae docet.
units.tr: The Papists interpret the blessing (εὐλογία) as the consecration, which, according to them, takes place by the murmuring of these five words: Hoc enim est sanguis meus ("For this is my blood"). Likewise: Hoc est enim Corpus meum ("For this is my body"). By the power of these words they hold that the wine is transubstantiated into the blood, and the bread into the body, of Christ. So Lyra and Dionysius: "The cup which we bless, that is, which we priests consecrate, is converted into the blood of Christ when, by the utterance of the sacred words, it is changed by us." For this consecration they cite Irenaeus, Ambrose, Cyril, and others. To this we reply: (1) this gloss on a so-called conversive consecration is most absurd, and most inept as well. For how do these things hang together? "The cup," that is, the blood in the cup; "which we bless," that is, which by consecration we convert into blood; "is the communion of the blood." What, I ask, is more inept than this gloss? (2) We acknowledge that the ancients sometimes speak in this way, that the bread is changed into the body of Christ by consecration; but this must not be understood of any essential change, by which the substance of the bread is converted into the substance of the body, but of a mystical and sacramental change, by which, through the intervention of blessing and consecration, the bread and wine are so changed that what was previously common and profane begins to be sacred, and so they are changed and converted from common and ordinary things into sacred ones. The consensus of orthodox antiquity teaches this.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Quaestio XII. An, contra, Nos recte ex hoc loco Transsubstantiationem impugnemus?
units.tr: Question XII. Whether, on the contrary, we rightly attack transubstantiation from this passage?

units.la: Argumentum nostrum hoc est: Ubi remanet substantia Panis,ibi nulla fit transsubstantiatio. At in Eucharistia post consecrationem remanet vera substantia panis. Ergo, &c. Maj.probatione non eget.Min.probatur inde: Quia Apostolus calicem benedictum & panem fractum vocat Calicem & panem: sic 1.Cor.11.26,27. Quotiescunque manducaveritis panem hunc,&c.
units.tr: Our argument is this: where the substance of bread remains, no transubstantiation takes place. But in the Eucharist, after consecration, the true substance of bread remains. Therefore, etc. The major needs no proof. The minor is proved thus: the Apostle calls the blessed cup "cup" and the broken bread "bread", as in 1 Cor. 11.26, 27: As often as you shall eat this bread, etc.

units.la: Excipiunt vocari panem vel quia panis fuerit, sicut vinum, ex aqua factum, vocetur aqua. Joh.2.9. vel quia videatur esse panis, uti Angeli, qui apparuerint in forma humana, homines dicantur; vel quia sub accidentalibus formis panis contineatur & lateat; vel quia nomine panis, panis coelestis indigitetur.
units.tr: They answer that bread is called bread either because it was bread, as wine made from water is called water (John 2.9); or because it seems to be bread, as angels who appeared in human form are called men; or because under the accidental forms of bread the substance is contained and hidden; or because by the name of bread the heavenly bread is designated.

units.la: Ad primum. 1. Vinum in nuptiis Cananaeis non simpliciter vocatur aqua,sed aqua vinum facta. 2. Transmutatio aquae in vinum coram oculis fiebat, & sensibus patebat. Transmutatio vini in sanguinem sensibus, rationi & Scripturae contraria est.
units.tr: To the first: (1) At the wedding in Cana the wine is not simply called water, but water made wine. (2) The change of water into wine took place before the eyes and was evident to the senses. The change of wine into blood is contrary to the senses, to reason and to Scripture.

units.la: Ad secundum. Quanquam nulla plane est consequentia: Angeli vocantur homines, quia videntur esse tales; E. panis eucharisticus vocatur panis, quia videtur tantum talis esse, non est; sequetur saltem, Paulum universam Ecclesiam Corinthiacam panem credidisse esse panem verum: sicut Angeli ideò vocantur viri, qui tales à Patriarchis crediti, pro viris habiti fuerunt.
units.tr: To the second: although there is plainly no valid inference here. Angels are called men because they seem to be such; therefore the eucharistic bread is called bread because it only seems to be such, which it is not. At the very least it would follow that Paul believed the whole Corinthian church took the bread to be true bread, just as the angels, who were believed by the patriarchs to be such, were held to be men.

units.la: Ad tertium: Responsio hæc absurdissima. Nam hac ratione dici posset, gladium esse vaginam, quia in vagina continetur; animam esse corpus, quia in corpore est; anguem herbam, quia latet in herba.
units.tr: To the third: this answer is most absurd. By this reasoning one could say that a sword is a scabbard, because it is contained in a scabbard; that the soul is a body, because it is in the body; or that a snake is grass, because it lies hidden in grass.

units.la: Ad quartum. Scriptura Corpus Domini aut Dominum nunquam vocat panem simpliciter, sed panem vivum aut panem qui de cœlo descendit, Joh.6.33.35.41. Cùm Apostolus ait, panem quem frangimus, innuit se loqui de pane visibili, qui in particulas frangeretur. At Corpus Christi invisibile est, nec in particulas dividi potest; sed impassibile est, secundùm ipsos. At joculare prorsus est, dicere sensum Apostoli esse, Panis, quem frangimus, i.e. Corpus quod non frangimus.
units.tr: To the fourth: Scripture never calls the body of the Lord, or the Lord himself, simply "bread", but "living bread" or "the bread which came down from heaven" (John 6.33, 35, 41). When the Apostle says "the bread which we break", he signals that he is speaking of visible bread, which is broken into pieces. But the body of Christ is invisible, and cannot be divided into pieces; according to them, it is impassible. To say that the sense of the Apostle is "bread which we break", that is, the body which we do not break, is utterly jocular.

units.la: Adhuc unum argumentum ex verbis istis fluit contra Transsubstantiationem. Sicut se habent cibi Dæmoniis consecrati, ad Dæmonia ipsa: Ita se habet calix consecratus & panis fractus, ad corpus & sanguinem Domini. Apostolus enim antithesin instituit inter Calicem & panem mensæ Domini, & cibos Idolis immolatos; inter Dæmonia & Dominum. At cibi Idolis consecrati non convertuntur substantialiter in Dæmonia; sed manent ab iis substantialiter distincti. E.& panis in corpus Domini, & vinum in sanguinem ejus non transubstantiantur; sed manent ab his distincta.
units.tr: Further, one more argument flows from these words against transubstantiation. As foods consecrated to demons stand toward the demons themselves, so the consecrated cup and the broken bread stand toward the body and blood of the Lord. For the Apostle sets up an antithesis between the cup and bread of the Lord's table and the foods sacrificed to idols, and between demons and the Lord. But foods consecrated to idols are not substantially converted into demons; they remain substantially distinct from them. Therefore bread is not transubstantiated into the body of the Lord, nor wine into his blood; they remain distinct from these.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: Quæstio XII. An hæc verba æquipolleant verbis promissionis, Hoc est corpus meum, Hoc est sanguis meus?
units.tr: Question XII. Whether these words are equivalent to the words of promise, "This is my body," "This is my blood"?

units.la: Verba promissionis in Institutione, Hoc est Corpus meum, ita explicamus, quòd Hoc denotet panem. Christum enim demonstrasse eâ particulâ illud ipsum, quod acceperit, gratiis actis fregerit, & fractum visibiliter porrexerit Discipulis. Hancce explicationem τὸ Hoc ulterius probamus ex præsentibus verbis Apostoli, qui τὸ Hoc interpretetur de pane: dicit enim, Panis quem frangimus. Loco ejus quod Christus dicit Hoc, Apostolus dicit, Panis quem frangimus.
units.tr: We explain the words of promise in the Institution, "This is my body," in such a way that "This" denotes the bread. For by that particle Christ pointed to the very thing he had taken, had broken after giving thanks, and had visibly handed to the disciples in its broken state. We further confirm this explanation of the "This" from the present words of the Apostle, who interprets the "This" as referring to the bread: for he says, "The bread which we break." In place of what Christ says, "This," the Apostle says, "The bread which we break."

units.la: Excipiunt Adversarii (qui per τὸ Hoc intelligunt non panem, sed vel speciem panis, vel individuum vagum, vel corpus Christi, vel panem & corpus Christi simul, seu totum ut loquuntur, complexum Sacramentale) propositiones istas duas, Hoc est corpus, & Panis quem frangimus est communio Corporis Christi; convenire quoad sensum, non esse tamen identicas. Nam differre subjectis & praedicatis. In verbis Christi Subjectum esse, Hoc, In verbis Pauli, Panis quem frangimus. Praedicatum in verbis Christi esse Corpus meum; in Pauli verbis, Communio corporis.
units.tr: Our opponents (who by "τὸ This" understand not the bread but either the appearance of bread, or an indefinite individual, or the body of Christ, or the bread and the body of Christ together, or, as they put it, the whole sacramental complex) object that these two propositions, "This is the body" and "The bread which we break is the communion of the body of Christ," agree in sense but are not identical. For they differ in subjects and predicates: in the words of Christ the subject is "This," in the words of Paul it is "the bread which we break"; the predicate in the words of Christ is "my body," in the words of Paul "the communion of the body."

units.la: R. Agnoscunt Adversarij verba Pauli convenire sensu cum verbis Christi, eorumque esse exegetica. Quod vero ex exegesi ista sequitur, non agnoscunt. Nos ita dicimus, Propositiones, quae quoad sensum conveniunt, idem quoque quoad sensum, habent subjectum & praedicatum. Et hoc nobis sufficit: Identitatem enim verborum nec Ipsi intelligimus, cum Propositiones istas dicimus identicas.
units.tr: Answer: Our opponents acknowledge that the words of Paul agree in sense with the words of Christ, and that they are explanatory of them. But what follows from this explanation they do not acknowledge. We say this: propositions which agree in sense have, in sense, the same subject and predicate. And this is enough for us: for we do not ourselves understand identity of words when we call these propositions identical.

units.la: XX.
units.tr: XX.

units.la: Quaestio XIV. An ex his verbis recte probetur Corporis Christi praesentia corporalis in pane, ejusq; in cum & sub pane oralis manducatio?
units.tr: Question XIV. Whether the bodily presence of Christ's body in the bread, and the oral eating of it in, with and under the bread, are rightly proved from these words?

units.la: Qui praesentiam corporalem & manducationem Oralem Christi in pane statuunt, ita argumentantur. Quod est communio corporis Christi, illi corpus Christi corporaliter, vel saltem indistanter, unitum est, atque in cum & sub eo, ore comeditur. At panis est communio corporis Christi. Ergo
units.tr: Those who hold a bodily presence and oral manducation of Christ in the bread argue thus: What is the communion of Christ's body, to that body of Christ is united bodily, or at least indistinctly, and it is eaten by the mouth in, with and under it. But bread is the communion of Christ's body. Therefore...

units.la: R. Panis non potest dici communio corporis sensu proprio. Aliud enim, proprie loquendo, est Panis qui frangitur; aliud, Corpus Domini, sive communio Corporis Domini. Ergo necessario quaerendus aut eligendus sensus alius. Sensus autem, quem Transsubstantiatores aut Consubstantiatores ponunt, nec verbis, nec scopo Apostoli convenit, Panis est communio Corporis, q.
units.tr: Reply: Bread cannot be called the communion of the body in the proper sense. For, properly speaking, the bread that is broken is one thing, and the body of the Lord, or the communion of the Lord's body, is another. Therefore another sense must necessarily be sought or chosen. The sense, however, which the Transubstantiators or Consubstantiators put forward agrees neither with the words nor with the purpose of the Apostle: Bread is the communion of the body, q.

units.la: Apostolus dixisset: Est talis Panis, cujus speciebus vel substantiae, Christi corpus indistanter est unitum, & cum cujus speciebus, vel cum quo, Corpus Christi ore participatur. Quis vero, cum indigitare vult, quod rei quae videtur, unita sit adhuc alia praestantior, quae non videtur, at simul detur & accipiatur; unquam ita loquatur? Amphora est communio vini: Crumena est communio pecuniae: pro, Crumena quam vides, est talis crumena, cui inest pecunia. Et, si maxime κοινωνίαν interpretentur non passive, Communionem; sed active, Communicationem (quae non est propria vocis significatio) tamen sensum, quem volunt, hinc nondum exsculpent. Aliud enim est, dicere: panem esse communicationem Corporis Christi; Aliud: Corpus Christi in, cum & sub eo communicari.
units.tr: The Apostle would have said: It is such bread, with whose species or substance the body of Christ is indistinctly united, and with whose species, or with which, the body of Christ is partaken by the mouth. But who, when wishing to point out that some more excellent thing, which is not seen, is united to the thing that is seen, yet is given and received at the same time, would ever speak like that? A jar is the communion of wine; a purse is the communion of money: meaning, "the purse you see" is such a purse as contains money. And even if they interpret κοινωνίαν not passively, as "communion", but actively, as "communication" (which is not the proper meaning of the word), they still will not thereby extract the sense they want. For it is one thing to say that bread is the communication of Christ's body, and another to say that Christ's body is communicated in, with and under it.

units.la: Si dicant, locutiones esse aequipollentes, Panem esse communicationem corporis, & panem corpus communicare. Resp. Et nos sano sensu concedere possumus, panem corpus Christi communicare, seu exhibere, atque communionis cum Corpore etiam organum esse exhibitivum: sed non physicum, ut isti volunt; verum morale.
units.tr: If they say the expressions are equivalent, "bread is the communion of the body" and "bread communicates the body": Reply: we too can, in a sound sense, concede that bread communicates or exhibits the body of Christ, and that the organ of communion with the body is also exhibitive; but not physically, as they wish, rather morally.

units.la: Praestat ita q; verba ista metonymicè explicare: Panem vid. esse communionem corporis Christi, h. e. Symbolum communionis corporis Christi, quo scil. nobis non solum significetur, sed & obsignetur communio, quam cum Corpore Christi habemus. Non diffitemur, esse etiam Unionem inter panem & corpus, ceu inter signum & rem signatam, quae vulgo relativa & Sacramentalis appellatur, atque non in eo consistit; quod panis & corpus se mutuo contingant, sed potius in eo, quod se mutuo respiciunt. Sed alienum est a Scripturae phrasi, Unionem illam relativam κοινωνίαν vocari, quae sit inter panem & corpus. Dein Unio illa non est unica corporis Christi communio, quae nobis in Coena proponitur: Christus enim, ut optime Melanchthon, non adest propter panem, sed propter hominem. Communio itaque Corporis Christi in S.Coena, longè excellentior & magis necessaria ea est, quâ Corpus Christi unitur per fidem communicanti, eiquesit alimonia spiritualis, & sine quâ salus non datur. Et hanc inprimis in hoc Textu nostro Apostolus intelligit.
units.tr: It is better also to explain these words metonymically: "bread is the communion of the body of Christ", that is, a symbol of the communion of Christ's body, by which is signified to us, and also sealed, the communion which we have with the body of Christ. We do not deny that there is also a union between bread and body, as between sign and thing signified, which is commonly called relative and sacramental, and which does not consist in this, that bread and body touch one another, but rather in this, that they mutually refer to one another. But it is foreign to the phrasing of Scripture to call that relative union, which exists between bread and body, "communion". Further, that union is not the sole communion of Christ's body that is set before us in the Supper: for Christ, as Melanchthon very well says, "is not present on account of the bread, but on account of the man." Therefore the communion of Christ's body in the Holy Supper, which is by far more excellent and more necessary, is that by which the body of Christ is united through faith to the communicant, which is for him spiritual nourishment, and without which salvation is not granted. And it is this especially that the Apostle understands in this our text.

units.la: XXI.
units.tr: XXI.

units.la: Quæstio XV. An nos ex his verbis præsentiam corporalem & manducationem Oralem recte impugnemus?
units.tr: Question XV. Do we rightly attack the corporeal presence and the oral manducation from these words?

units.la: Affirmatur: Argumenta sunt sequentia:
units.tr: It is affirmed, and the arguments are as follows:

units.la: 1. Talis nobis est κοινωνία corporis & sanguinis Domini in S. Cœna, qualis edentibus idolothyta erat commu-nio altaris & Dæmoniorum, quibus cibi isti erant im-molati. At communio hæc non erat oralis: Neque enim vel altare vel Dæmonia oraliter comederunt.
units.tr: 1. The communion of the body and blood of the Lord in the Lord's Supper is of the same kind as the communion [κοινωνία] of those who ate idol-offerings, that is, the communion of the altar and of demons, to whom those foods had been sacrificed. But that communion was not oral: for neither the altar nor the demons ate orally.

units.la: 2. De tali communione sanguinis & corporis Domini Apostolus agit, per quam fideles unum sunt cum Do-mino & inter se. Addit enim: Quoniam unus panis, unum corpus multi sumus. Atqui manducatio oralis non facit esse unum corpus cum Christo, & fidelibus. Nec enim reprobi & infideles, ut maximè oraliter communicent corpori Christi, secundùm Adversa-rios; unum fiunt cum Ipso corpus. Nam qui Spiritum Christi non habet, non est ejus. Rom. 8.9. quæ est participatio justitiæ cum iniquitate, &c. 2. Cor. 6.16.
units.tr: 2. The Apostle is speaking of such a communion of the blood and body of the Lord, through which the faithful are one with the Lord and with one another. For he adds: Since there is one bread, we who are many are one body. But oral manducation does not make us one body with Christ and the faithful. For, according to our opponents, the reprobate and unbelievers, even though they communicate orally with the body of Christ, do not become one body with him. For whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ is not his (Rom. 8.9), and what participation has righteousness with unrighteousness? etc. (2 Cor. 6.16).

units.la: 3. Eadem hîc intelligitur Communio, de quâ infrà, & quæ tàm in Baptismo, quàm in Cœnâ fit. Omnes, ait, in uno Spiritu, in unum Corpus baptizati sumus, & omnes in unum Spiritum potati sumus. 1. Cor. 12.13. Hæc autem non nisi Spiritualis est.
units.tr: 3. The same communion is understood here as the one spoken of below, which takes place both in Baptism and in the Supper. For in one Spirit, he says, we were all baptized into one body, and we were all made to drink of one Spirit (1 Cor. 12.13). But this communion is nothing other than spiritual.

units.la: Obječit 1. Gerhardus: Apostolum asserere, Panem esse Communionem corporis ipsius, non saltem benefi-ciorum: adeoque non intelligere Communionem Spiritualem, sed substantiæ ipsius corporis. R. Quasi verò Communio Spiritualis respiceret saltem Chri-sti beneficia & non Christum ipsum, seu Corpus Ipsius.
units.tr: Objection 1, by Gerhard: the Apostle asserts that the bread is the communion of his body itself, not merely of its benefits; and therefore he does not mean spiritual communion, but communion in the very substance of the body. Answer: as if spiritual communion regarded only the benefits of Christ and not Christ himself, or his body.

units.la: Obječ.
units.tr: Objection.

units.la: Distincte exprimi Communionem corporis & Communionem sanguinis Christi. Atqui si Communicatio saltem Spiritualis intelligeretur, non opus fuisse, distincte nominare corpus & sanguinem Christi, quia fides Christum uno actu complectatur, ut ex Joh.6. appareat. ℞. Etiam Joh. c. 6. Dominus distinguit manducationem carnis & bibitionem sanguinis sui, ubi tamen, Gerhardo ipso fatente, nonnisi de Spirituali Communione agitur.
units.tr: The communion of the body and the communion of the blood of Christ are expressed distinctly. But if only spiritual communication were meant, there would have been no need to name the body and blood of Christ separately, since faith embraces Christ in one act, as appears from John 6. Answer: Gerhard is also mistaken here. In John 6 the Lord himself distinguishes the eating of his flesh from the drinking of his blood, where nevertheless, as Gerhard himself concedes, only spiritual communion is in view.

units.la: Apostolum de tali κοινωνίᾳ corporis & sanguinis Christi loqui, quae omnibus Coenae convivis, dignis pariter & indignis conveniat, alloqui enim omnes Sacrâ Coenâ utentes, & hypocritas quidem nominatim, eosdem ab usu Idolothytorum in sequentibus versibus dehortando. ℞. Fallitur Gerhardus. Describit quidem Apostolus officium, finem & effectum Calicis & Panis Eucharistici; sed quoad legitimè utentes, i.e. eos, qui se probant, prout explicat c. seq. v. 28. Cùm igitur hypocritae & impii se non probent, illis panis quem frangimus, & calix cui benedicimus, corporis & sanguinis Christi communio non sunt.
units.tr: The Apostle is speaking of such a communion [κοινωνία] of the body and blood of Christ as belongs equally to all who sit at the Supper, worthy and unworthy alike; for he addresses all who use the holy Supper, and the hypocrites by name, dissuading them in the following verses from the use of idol-offerings. Answer: Gerhard is mistaken. The Apostle does indeed describe the office, purpose and effect of the Eucharistic cup and bread; but this is said with respect to those who use them lawfully, that is, those who prove themselves, as he explains in the following chapter, verse 28. Since therefore hypocrites and the impious do not prove themselves, the bread which we break and the cup which we bless are not a communion of the body and blood of Christ for them.

units.la: Sic indigni nil praeter Panem & Vinum acciperent, sicque contraherent reatum aeterni judicii, solius Elementaris Panis manducatione, quod absurdum. ℞. Non est absurdum: ad reatum enim judiciumque sufficit panis non Elementaris, sed Sacramentalis, adeoque signi corporis Christi, indigna & irreligiosa sumptio, de quo fusius alii.
units.tr: So the unworthy would receive nothing but bread and wine, and would thus incur the guilt of eternal judgment by eating only elemental bread, which is absurd. Answer: It is not absurd. For guilt and judgment arise not from the elemental bread but from the sacramental bread, that is, from the unworthy and irreverent taking of the sign of the body of Christ; on this others have written more fully.

units.la: XXII.
units.tr: XXII.

units.la: Quaestio XVI. An recte ex h.l. probetur, Fractionem panis in S. Coena esse necessariam?
units.tr: Question XVI. Whether it is rightly proved from this passage that the breaking of bread is necessary in the Holy Supper?

units.la: Ad exemplum Christi, panem frangentis in Coenâ, fractum quoq; esse in Ecclesia Corinthiacâ, patet ex hoc Textu.
units.tr: That, after the example of Christ, who broke bread in the Supper, the bread was also broken in the Corinthian church, is clear from this text.

units.la: Fractio haec Sacramentalis & μυστηριώδης fuit, utpote quâ significata est corporis Christi fractio, ut & hoc, quòd fideles, qui de uno Pane, per fractionem in multas particulas diviso, partiparticipant, unum corpus sint. Liquet hoc ex verbis Institu-tionis, 1. Cor. 11.24. hoc praeterea loco, quo Apostolus Calicem Eucharisticum vocat benedictum, & Panem describit à fractione: utrique symbolo ritum adjungens Sacramentalem, quo à Pane & Vino vulgari discernuntur. Cum itaque εὐχαρι- στία, quam Apostolus tribuit Calici, nemine contradicente, ritus Sacramentalis sit; quid ni fractio, quam tribuit pani, quoque talis esset?
units.tr: This breaking was sacramental and mysterious, inasmuch as by it was signified the breaking of Christ's body, and also this, that the faithful, who partake of one bread divided into many particles by the breaking, are one body. This is clear from the words of institution, 1 Cor. 11.24, and besides from this place, where the Apostle calls the Eucharistic cup blessed and describes the bread from its breaking, attaching a sacramental rite to each symbol, by which they are distinguished from common bread and wine. Since therefore the "thanksgiving" [εὐχαριστία], which the Apostle ascribes to the cup, is, with no one contradicting, a sacramental rite, why should not the breaking, which he ascribes to the bread, be of the same kind?

units.la: Excipiunt, Frangere hic esse distribuere. Frangere quandoque duplicem habere significationem, & praeter Fractionem etiam distributionem denotare (cuius generis verba pregnantia vulgò vocantur) facile concedimus. Sed in hac materia distributionem denotare non potest, quia in historia Institutionis distincte dicitur, fregit & dedit. Si fractio etiam distributionem denotaret, posteriori verbo non fuisset opus.
units.tr: They object that to break here means to distribute. We readily grant that to break sometimes has a double meaning and denotes, besides breaking, also distribution (words of this kind are commonly called pregnant). But in this matter it cannot denote distribution, because in the history of the institution it is distinctly said, "he broke and gave." If breaking also denoted distribution, the second verb would not have been needed.

units.la: Excipiunt praeterea, Fractionem panis non esse, quod volumus, repraesentativam Unitatis, sed multiplicitatis; & inferre corporis mystici in infinita schismata divisionem. Objiciant hoc Paulo diserte dicenti, fideles unum panem, per fractionem in plures particulas distributum, in Coena participantes, unum corpus esse. Viderint Adversarii, an hoc aeque de Coena, ut apud ipsos celebratur, dici possit: non enim de uno pane omnes edunt, sed singuli suum panem habent; si modo panis nomen meretur, quod accipiunt. Ex eodem polline multa crustula fiunt: unicuique suum datur: haec divisionem potius denotant, quam Communionem.
units.tr: They object further that the breaking of bread does not, as we maintain, represent unity but multiplicity, and that it implies a division of the mystical body into endless schisms. Let them object this to Paul, who plainly says that the faithful, partaking in the Supper of one bread distributed by breaking into many particles, are one body. Let the opponents see whether this can equally be said of the Supper as it is celebrated among them: for not all eat of one bread, but each has his own bread, if indeed what they receive deserves the name of bread. Many little crusts are made from the same flour; each is given his own. These signify division rather than communion.

units.la: XXIII.
units.tr: XXIII.

units.la: Quaestio XVII. An bene ex hac reijciatur Missa privata?
units.tr: Question XVII. Whether the private Mass is rightly rejected on this basis?

units.la: Missam privatam seu solitariam, ut vocant, ubi solus Sacerdos communicat, directe impugnant verba Apostoli, cum dicit, Panis quem frangimus; & iterum, Omnes ex uno pane participamus. Qui in historia Ecclesiastica versati sunt, notant: per multa secula neminem fuisse fidelium, cui quidem jus esset multa communionis; qui non in omnibus conventibus, quibus interererat, communicaret: postmodùm licitum quidem fuisse non-communicantibus interesse Sacræ Synaxi, ut tamen nusquam Cœna celebraretur sine communicantibus. Et quæ'nam coena, quod'nam convivium, quæ'nam communio in Missâ privatâ ? Scena est, non Cœna ejusmodi Missa. Sacerdos assistit altari, veste theatrali indutus, post multas gesticulationes, corporisque circumvolutiones, hostiam, manibus suprà caput elatis elevatam, à populo aversus ostendit. Audiunt, qui adsunt, quod non intelligunt: vident, quæ non participant: adorant, quod nesciunt. Nemo quicquam secum fert de epulo isto, nisi quod in oculis gerit, Hæc scil. Cœna & Communio Corporis Christi.
units.tr: The private or solitary Mass, as they call it, in which the priest alone communicates, is directly attacked by the words of the Apostle, when he says: "The bread which we break"; and again: "We all partake of one bread." Those versed in ecclesiastical history observe that for many centuries there was no one among the faithful who had a right to a share in the communion and yet did not communicate at every assembly he attended. Afterwards it was indeed permitted for non-communicants to be present at the sacred Synaxis, but the Supper was never celebrated without communicants. And what supper, what banquet, what communion is there in a private Mass? Such a Mass is a spectacle, not a Supper. The priest stands at the altar, clothed in theatrical vesture, and after many gestures and bodily turnings, he shows the host, lifted high above his head in his hands, with his back to the people. Those who are present hear what they do not understand; they see what they do not share in; they adore what they do not know. No one carries away anything from this feast except what he has seen with his eyes, namely, this Supper and Communion of the Body of Christ.

units.la: XXIV.
units.tr: XXIV.

units.la: Documenta.
units.tr: Lessons.

units.la: Superest, ut Documenta ex Textu hactenus exposito & vindicato eruamus. Id exequemur paucis. Docemur sequentia.
units.tr: It remains to draw out the Lessons from the text so far expounded and defended. We shall do this briefly. The following points are taught.

units.la: I. Ut maximè quædam cum Idololatris societas, in rebus hanc vitam spectantibus, licita sit; prohibita tamen omnis cum iis communio Religionis: non saltem quoad actus internos, sed & quoad externos. Et quantum ad hos, non saltem professio Idololatriæ, quæ fit Ore; sed & sacrorum Idololatricorum frequentatio, imò omnis consensus simulatio cavenda. Hic enim Apostoli scopus in Textu nostro. Prohibens Idololatriam v.14. non respicit saltem doctrinam, aut animi sensum; sed epulas, solennitates, congressus ad honorem Idolorum institutos, etiamsi nemo ad Confessionem adigeretur. Porrò solam Idolothytorum manducationem communionem cum Dæmoniis esse infert: ex quo concludit participationem talis mensæ cum participatione mensæ Domini subsistere non posse.
units.tr: I. Although some association with idolaters is lawful in matters that concern this life, all fellowship in religion with them is forbidden, not only in inward acts but also in outward ones. As far as outward acts go, one must avoid not only the profession of idolatry made with the mouth, but also attendance at idolatrous rites, and indeed every simulation of consent. This is the Apostle's aim in our text. In verse 14, when he forbids idolatry, he has in view not merely doctrine or the state of the mind, but the feasts, solemnities and gatherings instituted in honour of idols, even if no one were forced to make a confession. Moreover, he infers that the eating of things sacrificed to idols alone makes a fellowship with demons, and he concludes from this that participation in such a table cannot stand together with participation in the table of the Lord.

units.la: XXV.
units.tr: XXV.

units.la: II. Correptiones, ut tanto sint suaviores, laudibus temperandæ: Ut prudentibus loquor. Laudat Corinthios à prudentiâ, dum severè corripit.
units.tr: II. Reproofs should be tempered with praise, so that they may be the more gentle: I speak as to wise men. He praises the Corinthians for their prudence while he rebukes them sharply.

units.la: XXVI.
units.tr: XXVI.

units.la: III. Religio non per coactionem, sed persuasionem propaganda est. Apostolus Corinthiis doctrinam suam non obtrudit vi, nec, ut eam contra judicium mentis amplectantur, requirit; sed vult, ut de eâ priusipsi judicent, & judicio demùm suo probatam, profiteantur. Judicate vos quod ajo.v.15. Qui invitus credit, non credit, sed credere se simulat.
units.tr: III. Religion is to be propagated not by compulsion but by persuasion. The Apostle does not force his teaching on the Corinthians, nor does he require them to embrace it against the judgment of their minds; rather he wishes them first to judge it for themselves and, having tested it by their own judgment, to profess it. Judge for yourselves what I say (v. 15). He who believes unwillingly does not believe, but only pretends to believe.

units.la: XXVII.
units.tr: XXVII.

units.la: IV. Qui claves Regni coelorum in Ecclesiâ habent, fidem & obedientiam ab Auditoribus requirere possunt, coecum assensum non possunt. Hoc enim esset conscientiis imperare, seu, ut cum Apostolo loquar, fidei dominari, 2.Cor.1.24. Ea itaque, quae proponunt, subjiciant Auditorum judicio: judicate Vos Ipsi.
units.tr: IV. Those who hold the keys of the kingdom of heaven in the Church may require faith and obedience from their hearers, but they may not require blind assent. For this would be to lord it over consciences, or, to use the Apostle's words, to have dominion over your faith (2 Cor. 1:24). Therefore let them submit what they propose to the judgment of their hearers: judge for yourselves.

units.la: XXVIII.
units.tr: XXVIII.

units.la: V. De Rebus ergò fidei judicare, est quorumvis fidelium, adeoque etiam Laicorum. Hos enim non minùs ac alios alloquitur Apostolus dicens, judicate Vos ipsi. vid. Quaest.9.
units.tr: V. To judge matters of faith belongs to all the faithful, and therefore also to the laity. For the Apostle addresses these no less than the others when he says, judge for yourselves. See Question 9.

units.la: XXIX.
units.tr: XXIX.

units.la: VI. Judicium hoc fieri debet secundùm Verbum Dei, cujus Lectio proin populo non prohibenda sed commendanda, ut in eo exercitatos habeant sensus, & prudentes sint: Ut prudentibus loquor, judicate Vos ipsi.
units.tr: VI. This judgment must be made according to the Word of God. Therefore the reading of it is not to be forbidden to the people but commended, so that they may have their senses exercised in it and be wise: I speak as to wise men; judge for yourselves.

units.la: XXX.
units.tr: XXX.

units.la: VII. Judicium hoc non potest fieri sine Ratione, quae cum ingens Dei donum, ut in aliis, ita & hic adhibenda, ita tamen ut sese non extollat supra mysteria, sed modestè gerat, & quicquid potest, non contra sed pro veritate possit 2.Cor.13.8. vid Quaest.8.
units.tr: VII. This judgment cannot be made without reason. Reason, being a great gift of God, is to be used here as elsewhere, yet in such a way that it does not exalt itself above the mysteries but conducts itself modestly, and is able to do nothing against but for the truth (2 Cor. 13:8). See Question 8.

units.la: Consectar. Etiam ad Coenam non eundum rejectâ Ratione & stultâ cum credulitate, uti quidam volunt.
units.tr: Corollary. Nor is one to go to the Supper with reason rejected and with foolish credulity, as some wish.

units.la: XXXI.
units.tr: XXXI.

units.la: VIII. In Coena Res externa sunt duo symbola, Calix aequè ac Panis: neq; Coena aliter celebrari aut potest, aut debet, quàm exhibitione utriusq; Symboli. Con-
units.tr: VIII. In the Supper the external elements are two signs, the cup as well as the bread; nor can or ought the Supper to be celebrated otherwise than by the exhibition of both signs. Con-

units.la: Confess. Nobis propterea satis non est, quòd qui ad Communionem Ecclesiae Romanae Ecclesias Evangelicas invitant, concessum iri libertatem communicandi sub utraque promittunt, scil. pro bono pacis redimendo, & propter duritiem cordis nostri. Postulamus insuper, eam sententiam ut haereticam condemnari, quae statuit, Communionem sub una sufficere. vid. Quaest. 10.
units.tr: Confession. It is therefore not enough for us that those who invite the Evangelical churches to communion with the Roman Church promise that freedom to communicate under both kinds will be granted, namely in order to purchase peace and on account of the hardness of our hearts. We further demand that the opinion which holds that communion under one kind suffices be condemned as heretical. See Question 10.

units.la: XXXII.
units.tr: XXXII.

units.la: IX. Symbola per gratiarum actionem ita consecrantur, ut ab Usu communi ad sacrum segregentur.
units.tr: IX. The signs are consecrated by the giving of thanks in such a way that they are set apart from common use for a sacred purpose.

units.la: XXXIII.
units.tr: XXXIII.

units.la: X. Manent itaque quoad substantiam etiam post consecrationem, quod fuerunt. vid. Quaest. 11, 12.
units.tr: X. Therefore they remain, as to their substance, what they were even after consecration. See Questions 11 and 12.

units.la: XXXIV.
units.tr: XXXIV.
